title: Mani stones
hook: stones carved with mantras, piled along paths and passes

segments.voice: Yesterday, kora, the walk around the holy, and your line, walk the circle. Did one lap of your day slow down? Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

A trail climbs toward a high pass. No trees, thin air, wind that doesn't stop. And beside the path, a low wall that isn't really a wall: flat stones stacked together, more than anyone could count at a glance, some gray and plain, some painted in bright blue, red, yellow and white. Look closer and every one is carved. The same six syllables, over and over, cut into rock by hands you'll never meet. A walker coming up the trail steps to the left so the wall stays on her right, sets one more stone on the pile, and keeps climbing. Today: mani stones.
screen: `A WALL BESIDE A HIGH TRAIL.` → `EVERY STONE IS CARVED.` → `ONE MORE STONE ON THE PILE.`

segments.voice: First, what's carved. Mani stones usually carry om mani padme hum, the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, whom Tibetans call Chenrezig. Some carry other mantras, a prayer, or an image of a buddha. The name comes from the mantra's second word, mani, a jewel. Second, who makes them. Some are carved by skilled stone carvers, who sell or are paid for them. Some are cut by a family to mark a death, a birth, a recovery, or a hope. Some are scratched by a pilgrim with a nail and a lot of patience. Then they're left where people pass: at a pass, a bridge, a crossroads, the edge of a village, around a stupa. Over years, the piles grow into long walls, built by strangers who never met. Third, the idea underneath. Tibetan teachers say a mantra carved in stone keeps sounding. A prayer flag lets the wind carry its words; a prayer wheel lets the turning hand recite; a mani stone lets the rock do it, quietly, in every weather, for as long as it lasts. That's the sense of today's line: the stone chants. It isn't saying a rock has a voice. It's saying the wish carved into it doesn't stop when the carver goes home. Fourth, how to pass one. Travelers walk past mani walls keeping them on their right, the same clockwise respect as yesterday's kora. Stones are added, not taken. Taking one home as a souvenir would be taking someone's prayer. And a person carving their first stone is joining a long line of strangers, each adding one more wish for the beings who will walk this way.
screen: `OM MANI PADME HUM, CARVED.` · `CARVERS, FAMILIES, PILGRIMS.` · `A WISH THAT KEEPS SOUNDING.` · `KEEP IT ON YOUR RIGHT. ADD, DON'T TAKE.` · then, large: `THE STONE CHANTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you have a stone, a pebble, or even a scrap of paper and a pen. Slowly write one short line on it. If you'd like, write om mani padme hum, or a line from your own tradition, or just one word that holds a wish for others, like kindness. Write it slowly, one letter at a time, as if carving. Then hold it for a few breaths. If it's a stone, you might leave it somewhere people pass. The bell holds the time.
Mani stones. Stones carved with mantras, usually om mani padme hum, piled along paths, passes and stupas, and passed with respect on the right. Today's word.

Your line: the stone chants. Today, leave one good word somewhere it will outlast you for a while: a kind note on a fridge, a message in a card, a thank-you on a whiteboard. Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhist regions, stones carved with om mani padme hum and other mantras are left at passes, bridges, villages and stupas, where they build up into long mani walls; travelers pass them clockwise, keeping them on the right.

trapdoor: what you thought: decorated rocks by a trail.
what it means: stones carved with mantras, usually om mani padme hum, left where people pass as a lasting wish for all beings.
what a scholar hears: the same logic as prayer flags and prayer wheels: a mantra set in a material that keeps 'sounding' it, passed clockwise with respect.
